ui.aboutText: Ten chapters, in order of how important they are for everyday life and for exams (priority 1 = most important). Each chapter has rules, tables, examples and exercises. The answers are at the end of the book. The book teaches the Portuguese of Portugal: tu, você and o senhor as used there, estar a + infinitive, and the pronoun after the verb. Where Brazil is very different, it says so.
ui.aboutRule: Example sentences, tables, exercises and answers are in Portuguese, because Portuguese is what you are learning.

k1-intro.text: Portuguese has two verbs for “to be”: *ser* and *estar*. You need them to say who you are, where you are from, where you are and how you feel. Almost every first conversation uses them.

k1-why.text: English has one verb here and Portuguese has two, so you make this choice all the time. It can even change the meaning: *Ele é aborrecido* = he is boring. *Ele está aborrecido* = he is annoyed.
k1-why.title: Why is this so important?

k1-h1.text: Subject pronouns and the two verbs

k1-rule1.text: The verb ending already shows the person, so Portuguese often drops the pronoun: *Sou o Pedro. Estou em Braga.* Use the pronoun for contrast or to be clear: *Eu sou de Viseu e ela é de Faro.* There is no pronoun for “it”: *É grande.*

k1-m1.text: *Tu* is for friends, family, children and people your age. With a stranger, an older person or an official, people in Portugal often say *o senhor* or *a senhora* (or the name with a title: *a Dona Ana*) with the *ele / ela* verb form: *O senhor é o doutor Costa?* *Você* exists, but in Portugal it can sound cold or even rude, so as a learner use *o senhor / a senhora* when you are unsure. For two or more people use *vocês*. *Vós* is old-fashioned and no longer spoken.

k1-h2.text: ser: who or what someone or something is

head: Use
Example
cells: what someone or something is like

k1-m2.text: A plain job needs no article after *ser*: *Sou enfermeira*. With an adjective, use one: *Sou uma enfermeira muito boa.* Your age goes with *ter*, not *ser*: *Tenho 31 anos.* For a building or a town, *ficar* is also common: *O centro de saúde fica na Rua Direita.*

k1-err.text: For the place of a person or a thing, use *estar*, never *ser*.

k2-intro.text: We use the present tense for habits and facts, for what is happening now and for plans in the near future: *Moro em Lisboa. Trabalho no hospital. Amanhã vou ao médico.* In Portugal, for something happening right now you can also say *estou a + infinitive* (chapter 7).

k2-rule1.text: Every Portuguese verb ends in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* in the dictionary. Take off the ending and add the one for the person. The *eu* form always ends in *-o*.

k2-m1.text: The *-er* and *-ir* endings are the same, except with *nós*: *comemos*, but *partimos*. The *-ar* form with *nós* ends in *-amos*.

k2-h3.text: How often? Words that often go with the present

k2-m2.text: *Às segundas-feiras* means every Monday: *Às segundas trabalho em casa.* *Na segunda-feira* means the next Monday: *Na segunda-feira tenho consulta.*

k2-err.text: The form with *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* is only the dictionary form. In a sentence the verb needs the ending for the person.

k3-intro.text: Portuguese needs no helping verb like “do” in questions and negatives. A question is often the same sentence with a rising voice, and for a negative you put *não* before the verb.

k3-why.text: You ask questions all day in Portugal: at the Junta, at the *centro de saúde*, at the shop. And a clear *não* is useful too.
k3-why.title: Why is this so important?

k3-rule1.text: Take a normal sentence and let your voice rise at the end. Write only one question mark, at the end (no upside-down mark): *Falas inglês?* You can add *não é?* or *certo?* to ask for agreement.

k3-rule2.text: Question word + verb + subject, or add *é que* after it: *Onde moras? / Onde é que moras?*

head: Question word
Asks about
Example
cells: the way, what it is like
a price, an amount, a number

k3-m1.text: *Porque* (one word, no accent) starts a question: *Porque estudas português?* *Porquê* (with the accent) stands alone or ends the sentence: *Estudas português. Porquê?* The answer is *porque*: *Porque trabalho aqui.*

k3-rule3.text: Put *não* right before the verb: *Não trabalho hoje.* In a short answer you often say it twice: *Trabalhas amanhã? Não, não trabalho.*

k3-rule4.text: After the verb, Portuguese needs *não* before it as well: *Não tenho nada. Não conheço ninguém.* If the negative word comes first, there is no *não*: *Nunca bebo café. Ninguém sabe.*

k3-err.text: In English, two negatives cancel each other out. In Portuguese they don't: after the verb, *nada* and *ninguém* need *não* before the verb.

k4-intro.text: Every Portuguese noun is masculine or feminine, also words for things. Articles and adjectives must agree with it. The word for “there is / there are” is *há*.

k4-rule1.text: The ending of a noun usually tells you. For other endings, learn the word together with its article.

k4-m1.text: Common exceptions: *o dia, o problema, o idioma, o mapa* are masculine; *a mão, a foto* are feminine.

k4-rule2.text: Portuguese uses *o, a, os, as* also for things in general, where English has none: *A vida em Lisboa é cara.* In Portugal the article also goes before possessives and often before first names: *o meu telemóvel, a Ana, o João.*

k4-m2.text: Small words fuse with the article: *a + o = ao*, *de + o = do*, *em + o = no*, *por + o = pelo*; with *a*: *à, da, na, pela*. *Vou ao médico. Venho do trabalho. Moro na Rua Direita. Estou no hospital.*

k4-rule3.text: An adjective usually goes after the noun and agrees with it in gender and number: *o carro novo, a casa pequena, os carros novos.* Adjectives in *-e* or in most consonants have one form for both genders.

k4-rule4.text: *Há* means “there is” and “there are”, and it has only this one form. Use *está / estão* for a particular thing you already know.

k4-err.text: *Carro* is masculine, so the article and the adjective are masculine too. Learn every new noun with *o* or *a*.

k5-intro.text: The most common Portuguese verbs are irregular. The good news: there are only a few groups, and most verbs are irregular in the *eu* form only.

k5-m1.text: *Ter* is for age, hunger and more, where English uses “be”: *Tenho 31 anos. Tenho fome. Tenho frio. Tenho sono.* Listen for the difference between *ele tem* (one person) and *eles têm* (more than one): the plural has an accent.

k5-h2.text: Irregular only in the eu form

k5-rule1.text: Some verbs are irregular only with *eu*. All the other persons are regular.

k5-m2.text: *Saber* is to know a fact or how to do something: *Sei conduzir.* *Conhecer* is to know a person or a place: *Conheço a Marta. Conheço o Porto.*

k5-h3.text: Vowel and consonant changes in some verbs

k5-rule2.text: In these verbs the spelling changes only in the *eu* form. The other persons are regular.

k5-err.text: *Saber* is irregular with *eu*: *sei*. Learn the *eu* form together with the infinitive.

k6-intro.text: Portuguese has small pronouns (*me, te, o, a, nos, os, as, lhe, se…*). In Portugal they usually go after the verb, joined with a hyphen: *chamo-me, vejo-a*. This chapter also shows how to say what you like.

k6-rule1.text: *Gostar* is a regular *-ar* verb and always takes *de*: *Gosto de café. Gosto de ler.* With an article the two fuse: *Gosto do café, da cidade, dos vizinhos, das aulas.*

k6-m1.text: To agree: *Gosto de café. Eu também.* / *Não gosto de café. Eu também não.* To disagree: *Eu não.* / *Eu gosto.* To ask politely for something, use *gostava de*: *Gostava de marcar uma consulta, por favor.*

k6-rule2.text: These verbs have *-se* at the end in the dictionary: *levantar-se*. The pronoun changes with the person and, in Portugal, goes after the verb with a hyphen: *Levanto-me às sete.* It goes before the verb after *não, nunca, já, também, que, quem, onde, como…*: *Não me levanto cedo. Como te chamas?*

k6-m2.text: With an infinitive, the pronoun goes after the infinitive in Portugal: *Vou levantar-me cedo. Preciso de sentar-me.* After *não* it can go before the first verb: *Não me vou levantar.*

k6-rule3.text: An object pronoun replaces a person or a thing. A direct object answers “whom or what?”, an indirect object “to whom?”. In Portugal the pronoun follows the verb: *Vejo-a. Escrevo-lhe um email.*

head: Pronoun
Means
Example
cells: him, her, it; you (o senhor, a senhora)
to him, her, you / to them

k6-m3.text: Pronouns go before the verb after words that “pull” them: *não, nunca, já, também, que, quem, onde, porque*: *Não a vejo. Quem te ajuda?* After a verb ending in *-r, -s* or *-z*, *o / a* become *lo / la* and the ending drops: *fazer + a = fazê-la*; *fazemos + o = fazemo-lo*.

k6-err.text: In Portugal the pronoun normally follows the verb: *chamo-me*. *Me chamo* is the Brazilian order.

k7-intro.text: Many everyday meanings come from two verbs together. Only the first verb changes with the person. The second one stays in the infinitive.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
cells: have to: you or someone in particular
you have to: a rule for everybody

k7-rule1.text: The first verb takes the ending for the person; the infinitive never changes: *Tenho de ir. Temos de ir. Eles têm de ir.* Note the small word *de* after *ter*. People also say *ter que*, but *ter de* is the standard form.

k7-m1.text: *Não tens de vir* = it isn't necessary. *Não deves vir* = you shouldn't come. *Não podes vir* = you are not allowed or not able to come.

k7-rule2.text: This is the most common way to talk about plans. Use the present of *ir* and the infinitive, with no *a* and no *de*: *Vou pagar a renda amanhã.*

k7-h3.text: estar a + infinitive: what is happening right now

k7-m2.text: Use *estar a + infinitive* for the moment of speaking, not for the future: *Amanhã vou trabalhar* (not *estou a trabalhar*). In Portugal always say *estou a trabalhar*, with *a* and the infinitive. *Estou trabalhando* is the Brazilian form.

k7-err.text: After *ter* you need *de* before the infinitive. After *poder, querer, dever* and *ir* there is no small word, and the second verb stays in the infinitive: *Posso ajudar. Quero ir. Vou comprar.*

k8-intro.text: In Portugal, the everyday past tense for something that happened and is finished is the *pretérito perfeito* (simple): *Ontem fui às Finanças.* There is also a compound form with *ter*, but it means something different from the English “have done”.

k8-rule1.text: Take off *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* and add the endings. *-er* and *-ir* verbs have the same endings.

k8-m1.text: In Portugal the accent decides with *-ar* verbs: *falamos* = we speak, *falámos* = we spoke. *Falou* = he or she spoke, *fala* = speaks. Verbs in *-er* and *-ir* have no such pair.

k8-m3.text: *Ser* and *ir* have the same forms in this tense: *Fui ao médico* (ir). *Fui professor durante dez anos* (ser). The context tells you which one.

k8-rule3.text: The participle ends in *-ado* (*-ar* verbs) or *-ido* (*-er* and *-ir* verbs). With *ter* it describes something repeated or continuing up to now, not one finished event: *Esta semana tenho dormido mal.* It is not the English “I have done”.

k8-rule2.text: One finished action, even from today, takes the simple *perfeito*: *ontem, na segunda-feira, na semana passada, em 2019, há dois anos, hoje de manhã.* Use *ter* + participle only for a repeated or continuing action up to now: *ultimamente, esta semana, este mês, nos últimos dias.*

k8-err.text: *Ontem* is finished time, so use the simple *perfeito*. *Tenho + participle* is for actions that repeat or continue up to now.

k9-intro.text: The *imperfeito* describes the past: what things were like, what was going on and what used to happen. The *perfeito* tells what happened, one event after another.

k9-rule1.text: *-ar* verbs take *-ava*, and *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-ia*. The *eu* and *ele* forms are the same. With *nós*, *-ar* verbs have an accent: *falávamos*.

head: Use
Example
cells: a habit, what used to happen
age, time and weather in the past
an action that was going on

k9-m1.text: *Antes* + *imperfeito* is the usual way to say “used to”: *Antes morava em Lisboa.* *Costumar* + infinitive also works: *Costumava ir à praia.* *Ir* is regular here: *ia, ias, ia, íamos, iam.* For something in progress, Portugal also says *estar a*: *Estava a chover quando saí.*

k9-rule2.text: Think of a film. The *imperfeito* is the background: the scene and the weather. The *perfeito* is the action that moves the story on, and it interrupts the background.

k9-m2.text: A finished period with a clear length takes the *perfeito*: *Vivi dois anos em Lisboa.* A repeated habit in that period takes the *imperfeito*: *Em Lisboa apanhava o metro todos os dias.*

k9-err.text: Your age in the past is background, so it takes the *imperfeito*.

k10-intro.text: This chapter brings together four things you need at B1: the *futuro*, the *condicional*, the future subjunctive after *se* and *quando*, and your first present subjunctive.

k10-rule1.text: Add the endings to the whole infinitive; all verbs have the same endings. In speech, *ir* + infinitive (chapter 7) is more common; the *futuro* is typical for writing, formal speech and promises.

k10-rule2.text: It has the same stems as the *futuro*, with the endings *-ia, -ias, -ia, -íamos, -iam*. Use it for polite requests and advice: *Poderia ajudar-me? Gostaria de marcar uma consulta.* In formal writing a pronoun can go inside the verb (mesoclisis): *Dir-lhe-ei amanhã.* You only need to recognise it at this level.

k10-h3.text: se and quando: the future subjunctive

k10-rule3.text: For something that has not happened yet, Portuguese uses the future subjunctive after *se* and *quando*: *Se chover, fico em casa. Quando chegares, liga-me.* Take the *eles* form of the perfeito, remove *-ram* and add *-r, -res, -r, -rmos, -rem*.

k10-m1.text: Do not use the *futuro* or the present for a future time after *se* or *quando*: not *Se choverá*, not *Quando chegas amanhã*. The simple present after *se* is for facts and the present: *Se tens fome, come alguma coisa.*

k10-rule4.text: Start from the *eu* form of the present and swap the vowel: *-ar* verbs take *-e*, all others take *-a*.

k10-m2.text: Same person: infinitive. *Quero ir.* Different person: *que* + subjunctive. *Quero que venhas.* The subjunctive also follows *esperar que, é importante que, talvez, oxalá*: *Espero que o senhorio responda. Oxalá faça bom tempo.*

k10-err.text: For a future time after *se* or *quando*, use the future subjunctive: *chegares*, not *chegas* or *chegarás*.
